comments.text: As someone who has been a teacher for 7 years, and in education for 10, the public school system is okay. However, if you want your child to be successful, the parents need to supplement their child’s education at home. No teacher is able to teach a class of 30 students and do everything on their own. The biggest issue that I see is that parents expect teachers to do everything. They don’t want to parent. I’ve been cursed out more times than you can imagine by parents of students who I am trying to reach out to, to get help with their student. comments.text:
As someone who has worked in private education, it’s not always better. In states like Florida where there are looser standards for non-public schooling, parents can be promised customized curriculums, one-on-one or small-group instruction, technology integration, and on-par or higher standards for the staff… but these are often empty promises. Private schools, especially smaller ones that rely heavily on school choice vouchers, can end up with 20-student classrooms with little support staff, no school nurse, no school psychologist, no gifted program, and no remedial classes. These schools don’t fail kids and they don’t have them repeat grades. They let kids graduate who would not have met the requirements in public school. These schools concentrate kids with behavioral, intellectual, or other disabilities and disorders who can’t be properly accommodated for (or tolerated) at public schools. They end in classrooms with 20+ children that are often all struggling but are also on vastly different levels because again, they don’t hold kids back. You have one teacher and maybe a TA trying to teacher middle schoolers how to read and do basic arithmetic while also hoping that they can absorb some of the grade level content they’re supposed to be learning. These teachers and support staff and even the administrators are as underpaid and overworked as the public school staff except they often don’t have unions or government employee benefits. These kids have limited options in electives, don’t learn to use computers (but they all have iPads), they don’t get sex ed, they don’t get to play competitive sports, and they don’t have clubs. It’s a worse experience from every angle, at least at the school I worked at. I also work at a tutoring center and I think THAT is a worthwhile endeavor if parents really want individualized support.

Also, SEND YOUR KIDS TO PRESCHOOL. Get them learning letters and numbers early, get those fine motor skills started, get them used to the school environment. It is very easy to pick out which kindergartners went to preschool and which ones didn’t
